articles.author: Tom Perkins
articles.content: Experts say NIH research raises concerns about chemical companies’ influence on US agency’s pesticide division The US government’s top medical research agency has released three new studies linking glyphosate, the world’s most widely used pesticide and an active ingredient in Roundup, to cancer . The National Institutes of Health (NIH) findings contradict a controversial recent Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conclusion that the weedkiller is not a carcinogen, and deals a blow to the White House, which has been closely allied with Roundup’s producer, Bayer. The NIH’s three papers could have significant political and legal fallout. The EPA is in the process of a court-ordered re-evaluation of glyphosate’s cancer risks. The NIH findings generate new pressure for the EPA to find that the substance is linked to cancer, which would subject it to a modest increase in regulations. Continue reading...

articles.content: Tens of thousands of people experience strikes each year. What are the effects of a current five times hotter than the sun – and how can you keep safe? Caitlin Thomas recalls knowing that something terrible had happened but not fully understanding what. She and her partner had arrived at a music festival some 270km north of Melbourne in the early afternoon and began setting up their tents and a gazebo for shade when the sky suddenly turned dark and the rain became incredibly heavy. A huge gust of wind picked up and Thomas asked her partner to hold on to the gazebo so it wouldn’t fly away. “He then asked me to hold on to it also so he could crack open his beer.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Rafael Behr
articles.content: Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

Up until now, our knowledge of tidal levels has been limited. Tide gauges tell us about a specific location, and satellite radar measurements typically average across tens of kilometres. articles.content: Royal Court theatre, London Ryan Calais Cameron’s ‘true(ish)’ account of a charismatic freedom fighter’s plan to take a Zambian crew to the moon never quite lifts off Ryan Calais Cameron has proved himself a playwright of stratospheric talent. His previous plays For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy and Retrograde both streaked their way into the West End. This new one is filled with mighty ambition but does not lift off in the same way. It is based on what he calls a “true(ish)” story. The figure of Edward Mukuka Nkoloso (Lucian Msamati) is taken from Zambian history. A freedom fighter for the nation’s independence in the 1960s, he set up a national academy for science and trained a group of “afronauts” in the hope of beating the US and the Soviet Union in the race to reach the moon. Nkoloso, a kind of Dead Poets Society inspiration figure here, picks 17-year-old Martha (Ama Qamata) for the mission. Continue reading...

articles.content: The trees have been functionally extinct in the US for nearly a century. But new techniques are creating plants resistant to the parasitic blight that almost wiped them out Jeff White is starstruck by a tree. The farmer and environmentalist from rural Maryland has an affinity with the American chestnut but has never seen one stretch from root to sky like this one. “About how tall is it?” he asks. “Over 70ft [21 metres],” says Cassie Stark, director of science implementation for the American Chestnut Foundation (TACF). “Just incredible,” White says, his gaze fixed upwards. “I’ve never seen one so tall and so healthy.” ‘Thompson’, above left, is an unusually tall specimen of an American chestnut, a now-rare species once ubiquitous in the US. Jeff White next to ‘Gladys’, a thriving 15-metre-tall pure American Chestnut in Virginia’s Lesesne forest Continue reading...

articles.author: Helen Pilcher
articles.content: We’ve been training for this mission for years – solving problems, defusing tensions, keeping everyone fed – and we’d absolutely smash it Nasa is hiring and I’m over the moon. The US space agency is recruiting its next cohort of astronauts to work on the lunar surface and “help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure”. Applications close on 3 December. This isn’t the only job I’ve been swooning over lately. I can’t tell you how many hours I’ve lost to posts about deliciously distant jobs: running the world’s southernmost post office in Antarctica, where staff double as penguin counters, or minding the Great Blasket island off the coast of County Kerry, where the northern lights sometimes shimmer over the North Atlantic. All of it bathed in a warm, rosy glow. In our always-on world, swapping the inbox for an island – or, for the truly frazzled, the moon – seems less like a job and more like a wellness retreat. Helen Pilcher is a science writer and the author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side Effects Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.content: Being so close to the sun, the smallest planet in the solar system is also one of the most difficult to spot This week offers a good opportunity to spot Mercury, the smallest planet in the solar system and one of the most difficult to observe. On 20 November, it reached “greatest western elongation”, the point at which it appears farthest from the sun in the morning sky. The planet remains well placed for observation over the next few mornings. The chart shows the view looking east-south-east from London at 0630 GMT on 24 November. Mercury appears low above the horizon, while the much brighter planet Venus shines higher in the sky, close to Spica, the brightest star in the constellation of Virgo, the virgin. Continue reading...

articles.author: Huw Green
articles.content: Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it? Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill? Continue reading...

articles.author: Kayode Akintola
articles.content: The outbreak in DR Congo is shaping up to be the worst ever, but the support of local faith leaders – and adequate funding – will be needed to bring it under control Ebola is terrifying: I know, because I lived through the world’s worst outbreak of the disease . That was in west Africa between 2013 and 2016, when anyone infected by the virus had a nearly 40% chance of dying . There were 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths then. Now a rare strain of Ebola is spreading in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, much more quickly than a decade ago in Sierra Leone, Liberia and neighbouring countries. It is the 17th outbreak in DR Congo and already its worst, with more than 5,000 deaths . The UN is warning that the spread of the disease is outstripping the response, and it is widely expected to become the worst Ebola outbreak in history. There is no proven vaccine or treatment yet for the Bundibugyo variant; almost 50% of those infected have died . Continue reading...

articles.content: Since the spacecraft’s 1977 launch, our wonderful and terrible species has done great damage to our planet. Voyager has offered us a clear view of ourselves Imagine traveling nonstop for 49 years, alone in the dark with no destination in sight, powered by curiosity and engineering. Further imagine making that journey not at bullet train or jet plane speed, but much faster: at 37,800 miles per hour, free from friction in a vast sea of cold, soundless space, bombarded by radiation and cosmic rays yet still able to communicate with folks back home. Continue reading...

articles.content: Nasa sent the Voyager 1 and 2 probes into space almost 50 years ago to explore the outer reaches of our solar system. Now Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object from Earth, is about to reach a distance of one light-day away from our planet. To find out more about its astonishing journey, Madeleine Finlay hears from Jim Bell, a planetary scientist and professor at Arizona State University’s school of Earth and space exploration. He explains the seismic impact the mission has had on our understanding of the solar system, and where Voyager 1 could be heading now it has left the heliosphere Continue reading...
